name: Sydney
meta_description: TDSC investigative consulting in matters touching Sydney: NSW court and licensing context, ASX-listed and private company diligence, asset tracing support.
hero_lede: Sydney is Australia's largest city and its main financial centre, and investigative work connected to it runs under New South Wales law as well as Commonwealth law. TDSC scopes Sydney matters around NSW licensing, surveillance and evidence rules, and coordinates licensed NSW investigators where fieldwork is needed.
intro: Sydney, the capital of New South Wales, is Australia's largest city and its principal centre for banking, funds management, insurance and professional services. The Australian Government's Centre for Population, drawing on ABS data, puts Greater Sydney at about 5.56 million people in 2023-24, with a projection of about 5.65 million for 2024-25. The Australian Securities Exchange and the Reserve Bank of Australia are based in the city, and the major banks, superannuation funds and global investment firms maintain large operations in the CBD and North Sydney. Port Botany and Sydney Airport make the city a gateway for trade and travel with Asia and the Pacific, and technology, property, education and media are significant sectors.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Sydney because it is where much of Australia's capital is raised and deployed, and where many of its largest companies, funds and professional advisers are based. Foreign investors and lenders need to understand Sydney-based founders, fund managers and private companies before committing capital. Litigants in the NSW Supreme Court and the Federal Court need background research and asset tracing to support claims and enforcement. Employers face misconduct allegations that must be investigated fairly. And because private investigators in New South Wales must be licensed and are bound by strict surveillance rules, the method of gathering information matters as much as the information itself.

matters.title: Private company and founder diligence
matters.text: Researching Sydney-based private companies, founders and fund managers ahead of investment, using ASIC extracts, court records, insolvency notices and open sources, and paying particular attention to prior failed companies, director disqualifications and related-party dealings that may not appear in a pitch deck.

matters.title: Asset tracing for NSW proceedings
matters.text: Identifying real property, company interests and other assets in New South Wales held by a judgment or award debtor, using NSW title searches, ASIC records and litigation history, so counsel can assess freezing orders and enforcement in the Supreme Court or Federal Court.

matters.title: Financial services misconduct
matters.text: Supporting firms and their counsel where misconduct by advisers, traders or intermediaries in Sydney's financial sector is suspected, including background on individuals, reviews of regulatory banning and enforcement history, and mapping of connected entities that may have received funds.

matters.title: Workplace investigations under NSW rules
matters.text: Scoping workplace misconduct investigations for employers with Sydney staff, with attention to the NSW workplace surveillance and surveillance devices regimes, procedural fairness, and the need for any interviews or evidence gathering to stand up in the Fair Work Commission or the courts.

matters.title: Property and development counterparties
matters.text: Reviewing Sydney developers, builders and property syndicates for investors and lenders, including their corporate histories, phoenix activity indicators, building defect and insolvency litigation, and regulatory actions, in a market where development structures often use single-purpose companies.

local_context.title: NSW Supreme Court and Federal Court
local_context.text: Most large commercial disputes in Sydney are heard in the Supreme Court of New South Wales, whose Equity Division runs specialist lists including the Commercial List and the Technology and Construction List, or in the Federal Court of Australia's Sydney registry. Both courts have supported international arbitration: the Federal Court enforces foreign awards and has issued subpoenas in aid of Australian-seated arbitrations. Freezing and search orders are available from both courts where a real risk of dissipation is shown.

local_context.title: ACICA and arbitration in Sydney
local_context.text: The Australian Centre for International Commercial Arbitration administers cases mainly under the ACICA Arbitration Rules 2021 and Expedited Arbitration Rules 2021, in effect since 1 April 2021, and has announced updated rules for 2026. Sydney is an established seat, and NSW Supreme Court decisions have generally upheld arbitration agreements, including clauses that misname the appointing body. Research for arbitrations is scoped around what the tribunal will need to see.

local_context.title: NSW investigator licensing
local_context.text: In New South Wales, private investigators must hold a Class 2E licence issued by NSW Police under the Security Industry Act 1997 and the Security Industry Regulation 2016. The Security Licensing and Enforcement Directorate issues licences, audits licensees and refers possible offences to police. Applicants need at least a Certificate III in Investigative Services and must meet fitness and probity requirements. Any Sydney fieldwork commissioned through TDSC is carried out by appropriately licensed NSW investigators.

local_context.title: NSW surveillance and evidence rules
local_context.text: The Surveillance Devices Act 2007 (NSW) restricts listening, optical, tracking and data surveillance devices and the communication of recordings, and recent reforms tightened rules on covert tracking. Evidence gathered unlawfully can be excluded under section 138 of the Evidence Act 1995 (NSW); in Kadir v The Queen [2020] HCA 1, footage from cameras an investigator installed without consent was excluded. Separate NSW workplace surveillance legislation governs monitoring of employees.

local_context.title: Property and corporate records
local_context.text: Land titles in New South Wales are recorded on the Torrens register, and title searches can be obtained through authorised information brokers, showing the registered proprietor and dealings such as mortgages and caveats. Company information comes from ASIC's national register. Sydney is also home to the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption, whose public reports on state public sector conduct are a useful source in procurement and government-facing reviews.

tdsc_approach: TDSC handles Sydney matters from Nashville and has no office or licence in Australia. Engagements begin with a review of which records and rules apply: ASIC and ABN records, NSW title searches, Supreme Court and Federal Court files, insolvency notices, regulatory actions and NSW integrity body reports. Where the matter needs interviews, attendance at addresses or observation, TDSC coordinates Class 2E licensed NSW investigators and agrees the method with the client's Australian lawyers, so that the Surveillance Devices Act and evidence rules are respected and results remain usable in court. Personal information is handled with the Privacy Act 1988 in mind, and reports separate verified facts from inference.

faqs.q: Does an investigator working in Sydney need a NSW licence?
faqs.a: Yes. Private investigation work in New South Wales requires a Class 2E licence under the Security Industry Act 1997, issued by NSW Police and overseen by the Security Licensing and Enforcement Directorate. TDSC does not hold an Australian licence, so any Sydney fieldwork is carried out by appropriately licensed NSW investigators coordinated by TDSC.

faqs.q: Can covert video be used in a NSW court?
faqs.a: Only if it was obtained lawfully, and even then the court has discretion. The Surveillance Devices Act 2007 (NSW) restricts optical surveillance on private premises without consent, and section 138 of the Evidence Act 1995 (NSW) allows exclusion of improperly obtained evidence. The High Court excluded such footage in Kadir v The Queen in 2020.

faqs.q: Can we find out who owns a property in Sydney?
faqs.a: Generally yes. New South Wales operates a Torrens title register, and a title search shows the registered proprietor and registered interests such as mortgages and caveats. Where property is held through a company or trust, ASIC records and other sources are used to identify those behind the registered owner, with limits on what can be confirmed.

faqs.q: Which court will hear a large commercial dispute in Sydney?
faqs.a: Usually the Supreme Court of New South Wales, through the Equity Division's specialist lists, or the Federal Court of Australia where federal law or jurisdiction is engaged. The choice is for counsel. TDSC supports either with background research on parties and witnesses and with asset identification ahead of freezing or enforcement applications.

faqs.q: Is Sydney a suitable seat for international arbitration?
faqs.a: Sydney is an established seat, supported by the International Arbitration Act 1974 and courts that generally enforce arbitration agreements and awards. ACICA administers cases under its 2021 rules and has announced new rules for 2026. TDSC does not advise on seat selection, which is a matter for counsel, but supports research in Sydney-seated proceedings.
